title: The 'Flying Saucer' Started With a Guy From Boise
excerpt: The Pentagon’s UFO files get all the attention, but Idaho’s link to the first flying saucer sighting goes back to 1947.
content:
Since May of 2-26, the Pentagon has now posted seven batches of declassified UFO files. It's comical to see all the snarky social media comments pointing out the flip in the narrative regarding the very existence of UFOs. All these years, the government has denied their existence. NOW they're suggesting they're real, and nobody seems to care. People are understandably more concerned with paying bills in the current economy than a potential alien invasion.

READ MORE: WATCH: South Idaho Couple Captures Circular UFO With ‘Tail’

While I was doing my own research on the phenomenon, I found an interesting link between Boise, Idaho, and the first flying saucer report. Long before Pentagon reports or even the Roswell incident, it looks like the whole flying saucer thing started with a guy from Boise.

Kenneth Arnold's 1947 Flying Saucer Sighting

On June 24, 1947, Boise businessman and pilot Kenneth Arnold was flying near Mount Rainier in Washington. He reported nine shiny objects racing past the mountain at what he estimated was at least 1,200 miles an hour.

READ MORE: Idaho Witness Reports Swarm Of Orb UFOs Over Sand Dunes

The next day, he told his story to the East Oregonian newspaper in Pendleton. Arnold said the objects moved like a saucer skipped across water. He was talking more about the way they flew than he was about their shape. Headline writers picked up the phrase and ran with it. The "flying saucer" was born.

The 1947 Flying Saucer Sightings Over Idaho

Ten days later, the reports hit home. On July 4, United Airlines Flight 105 left Boise for Seattle. Minutes after takeoff, the crew reported a formation of discs over Emmett. Before the flight, the captain had joked he'd believe in the discs when he saw them.

Idaho Statesman aviation editor Dave Johnson went looking for himself. On July 9, he reported a black, darting disc high over Boise and shot 8mm film of it. The film showed a faint dot, at most.

Then came the Twin Falls saucer hoax. On July 11, a 30-inch disc with a Plexiglas dome turned up in a Twin Falls yard, and the FBI and Army intelligence came running. Later that day, four teenage boys admitted they built it as a joke.

When the Associated Press looked back at Idaho's biggest stories of the year, flying saucers topped the list.

What Happened to Kenneth Arnold?

Arnold co-wrote a 1952 book about his sighting and spent years talking about it. In 1962, he won the Republican nomination for Idaho lieutenant governor. He lost in the general election. He died in 1984.

Almost 80 years later, the government is finally opening its UFO files. The Pentagon says its UFO website has had more than a billion hits. But people seem to care less about UFOs and are much more worried about $4.58 a gallon for gas.

Honestly, I get it. Alien invasions can wait. A full tank can't.
